persons.name: A O T Breed
persons.note: A CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO PAPER OF 1833-1835 PRINTS THIS PERSON BY NAME IN THE TOWN. Read from newspaper_1833_1835. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1b), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. newspaper_1833_1835 names this person at Chicago by 4 February 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Breed, Mrs. Amanda | Letter. | January 12, 1877. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0443, printed page 179), admitted 1877-01-12 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Breed' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins A. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

persons.name: Samuel Jackson
persons.note: INDEPENDENTLY CORROBORATED RESIDENT. Originally documented in Chicago post-office evidence; independent resident research now corroborates the identity. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Jackson, Samuel' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 22 October 1834, column 8 — dated 1834-10-22. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Jackson, Samuel” (tax_1833_049, line 101). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Jackson' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “Samuel [C]. Jackson” (33SQ-GYYJ-93G, printed page 207, line 5). This project has ruled the head a MATCH for this person: the full name agrees, it is unique on both sides, and a discriminator independent of the name — directory persistence — separately places the same person in Chicago after the 1840 book was taken. Under the rule that decided it (L6 matched), by the crosswalk's own ladder (data/research/census_1840/resident_crosswalk.json). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

citations.citation: Chicago · July 1835: Building Inventory and Architectural Reconstruction Specification. Prepared for Kevin Haas, August 2026.
what_it_supplies: A 665-roof production target with independently reconcilable group, district, level, and construction totals.
Thirty-five architectural family definitions with dimensional and massing bands.
District character, spacing, variation, finish, and chronology constraints for a July 1835 reconstruction.

citations.citation: The first Chicago Catholic church register — Father John Mary Irenaeus St. Cyr's marriage register and his death and burial page — as printed and annotated in the *Illinois Catholic Historical Review*, vol. 4 (July 1921 - April 1922), and republished in two pages by the Genealogy Trails Transcription Team. 128 dated marriages of 1834-1839, each naming groom, bride, witnesses and officiating priest, and 11 deaths and burials of June 1834 to March 1837.

transcribes.work: The first Chicago Catholic church record, kept by Father J. M. I. St. Cyr from 1833 and continued by Fathers Bernard Schaeffer and Timothy O'Meara to 1839
transcribes.note: THE ORIGINAL, and nobody in this project has seen it. What is read here is a 1921-22 article that prints the marriage entries and the death entries and comments on them. The article itself says the death record 'is contained on a single page' of the book.

transcribes.work: Illinois Catholic Historical Review, vol. 4 (July 1921 - April 1922)
transcribes.note: The layer actually read, at one further remove: the Genealogy Trails team transcribed these two pages out of the Review and this project read the transcription. Every record citing this source is graded transcription_mediated, twice over.

what_it_supplies: 128 marriages at Chicago (125 of them) between 1834 and 1839, each dated, and each naming its witnesses BY NAME — 513 named readings of people standing at a named place on a named day
six marriages IN THE SCENE YEAR, which with their witnesses put twenty named people in Chicago on five days of 1835
eleven deaths and burials, four of them in 1835, including the death of Thomas Owen, agent of the Indians, at Chicago on 15 October 1835
the register's own arithmetic — 22 St. Cyr marriages, 18 Schaeffer, 87 O'Meara, 1 Plunkett — which verifies any reading of it without the book
the dates bounding each priest's time at Chicago, which is what makes an unsigned entry attributable
the Irish, French and German Catholic population of the town, which is the part the poll books and letter lists reach least well
what_it_does_not_supply: any address, lot, dwelling or workplace — the register places nobody anywhere in the town
any age, except for three infants and one nine-year-old on the death page
the baptisms. The article tallies 282 of them by these same priests and prints none; that register is T-0503's object and is not in this source
residence. A marriage at Chicago on a day of 1835 is presence on that day, and presence is not residence
reliable spelling. The article says so itself: a French and German priest writing Irish and English names, and an Irish priest writing French and German ones
